job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Zoe Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts at five, because I live above the family bakery in Stuttgart and the ovens are already warm. I help with the morning rush, then I go upstairs and do applications and the bakery's weekly numbers, which I've started to run with an AI tool. My parents, Ingrid and Wolfgang, have three shops and nineteen staff. I finished business administration with a finance focus in the summer with the top grade, and I interned at a food wholesaler and at a mid-size tax firm. I haven't got an offer yet, because I'm being picky, and I'm not sure I'll end up outside the bakery at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it was oversold, and now people can get back to real work. I'd tell the staff that the ordering assistant I set up is useful but isn't magic. I'd tell my parents to keep investing in the ovens, since bread still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel good, very steady. I use these tools daily, so I know their limits. The market is wide open for graduates with my profile, and I could be doing the books at any one of fifteen firms nearby. My only private question is whether I want a corporate desk or the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep running the bakery's numbers with the tool, finish interviewing at two firms and make a decision by January. I'd also push my father to price our pretzels properly, because the margin is poor. I've got over six months saved and no debt, so I'm in no hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit restless. I'm 23, I have the top grade and a family business behind me, and I still can't decide. That's a good problem, but it's still a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Papa, honestly. Wolfgang wants me to take over the bakery one day, but he won't say so. My mother Ingrid says do what you love. I have a feeling I'll disappoint one of them whichever way I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother Oma Berta, who started the first shop, and my old thesis supervisor, Professor Keller. Oma says family comes first and bread comes second. Keller says take the outside job for two years and learn how a larger firm runs. I think Keller's right.

I'd tell my parents to keep investing in the **ovens**, since bread needs people.
think: I use the tools daily, so I know their **limits**.
My private question is whether I want a **corporate desk** or the bakery.
do: Keep running the bakery's **numbers** and finish interviews at two firms by January.
Push my father to **reprice the pretzels**, since the margin is poor.
feel: **Calm** and restless: a good problem, but still a problem.

Daily AI use leaves her unthreatened.

Keep running the bakery's weekly numbers with the AI tool
Reprice the pretzels with her father to lift the margin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's use it well, and I'd say the businesses that adapt win. At the bakery I'd say we should let the tools do the ordering and forecasting so people can spend time with customers. I'd say it in the trade association too, where some owners are fearful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the basic jobs in finance get automated, so the graduate market becomes tighter and smarter. The tax firm where I interned already used software for the returns, and the juniors checked them. I think I'm well placed because I use the tools and I understand businesses. But I'd feel for the ones who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the bakery as a proving ground. I'd set up the tools for ordering, waste tracking and rota planning, and see what we save. If it works, I'd offer it to other small bakeries and cafés. And I'd keep my outside options open by taking a job at a firm for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. It's a wave and I'm already on the board. I feel lucky, and I try not to be smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waste tracking is the first, and ordering. We throw out about fourteen percent of the bread every day at our bakery, and a forecast would cut that a lot. I'd tell friends to find a small business that wants help and just try something. The tools are cheap, the experience isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say go find a place where you can use it for real. Don't wait for a firm to hire you to learn it. And pick a business where the owner will let you try things, even a small one.

say: I'd say **businesses that adapt** win, and let tools do the ordering.
I'd speak at the **trade association**, where some owners are fearful.
think: Basic finance jobs get automated, so the graduate market becomes **tighter and smarter**.
I'm well placed because I use the tools and **understand businesses**.
do: Use the bakery as a **proving ground** for ordering, waste tracking and rotas.
Offer the system to **other small bakeries** if it works.
feel: **Calm**: a wave, and I'm already on the board.
S1.quote: We throw out about fourteen percent of the bread every day at our bakery, and a forecast would cut that a lot.
fieldNote: The family **bakery** is both her safety net and her lab.
Daily AI use turns change into opportunity.

steps.text: Set up AI ordering and waste tracking at the three bakery shops
Offer the system to other small bakeries and cafes
Take a finance job for a year or two to learn more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious and we need to protect people and let businesses adapt at the same time. I'd say it carefully, because panic helps nobody. At home I'd say to my parents that we need a plan for the bakery and the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be nervous. Two years isn't enough for anyone. My degree and my skills are in thinking work, and that goes first. The bakery is hands-on, which helps, but the ordering, the books and the marketing would all change, and I'd have to run them with tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery becomes the centre. I'd put the family business first, with savings in a safe place. I'd also use my tools to cut costs, and I'd try to make the bakery more resilient, with a loyalty scheme and a delivery service. I'd keep the outside job search for income, but loosely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit on edge. It's quick and it's big. But I'm used to adjusting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have meetings every week with my parents. We'd list what could go wrong and what we'd do. I'd call the other bakers I know and ask them to share costs on a delivery van. I think community is how small businesses survive a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my parents, I'm here and the business is the thing we hold on to. I'd say to Oma Berta, don't worry. And I'd tell the staff the truth, so they trust us.

say: I'd say it's serious and **panic helps nobody**.
I'd tell my parents we need a **plan** for the bakery and the staff.
think: Two years isn't enough, and my skills in **thinking work** go first.
The bakery's ordering, books and marketing would **change** too.
do: Put the **family bakery** first, with savings in a safe place.
Add a **loyalty scheme** and delivery service to make the shops resilient.
feel: **Uneasy** and on edge: it's quick and big, but I'm used to adjusting.
S2.quote: I think community is how small businesses survive a shock.
fieldNote: The **family bakery** becomes the centre of her plan.
Her adaptability shows in practical steps: delivery, loyalty and shared costs.
She would be **honest with staff** so they trust the family.

steps.text: Hold weekly planning meetings with her parents about the bakery
Launch a loyalty scheme and delivery service for the shops
Share a delivery van cost with other local bakers
Keep the outside job search going loosely for income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway and the smart move is to start now. I'd say to the staff that we'll use the tools to make the work easier, not to remove anyone. I'd tell friends to take it seriously and not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have time to build something. I'd work for a firm for a bit, then take on the bakery and grow it. By the time AGI arrives I'd have a business, savings and a lot of practice with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a job for two years at a firm that's good with technology, then bring what I learn back to the bakery. I'd save a lot. And I'd add a second business line to the bakery, like catering, so we're not just selling bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I've got energy for it. I think I'm built for this kind of challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's all hands on the bakery. With five, I can afford to go outside first, learn, and return stronger. I'd probably buy a small property for the next shop, because land isn't something AI changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd treat the first job as an apprenticeship. In my family we believe in learning a craft before you run it. That applies here, too.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent runway** and the smart move is to start now.
I'd tell staff the tools will make **work easier**, not remove anyone.
think: I have time to build something, a **business**, savings and tool practice.
By the time AGI arrives I'd be **ready**, with practice and a cushion.

S3.quote: In my family we believe in learning a craft before you run it.
fieldNote: Five years fit her **traditional apprenticeship** instinct: learn outside, then lead the bakery.

steps.text: Work two years at a firm that is good with technology
Add catering as a second business line at the bakery

Save a large share of every payslip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is lots of time and we should teach people the tools now. I'd say the bakery is still the right place to bet, because people like a person behind the counter. I'd tell Papa he can relax a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel very comfortable. A decade is a career. I'd run the bakery by then, probably, and we'd use machines for a lot of it, though the shops need people. I'd be 33 with a business and perhaps a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work outside for two or three years, then move into the bakery and take over the numbers and strategy. Marry, ideally, and have a family. I'd build up the bakery to five shops and a small online business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Lots of energy. I'd say this is the best-case version, and I'd want to use it to the full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the time on being good at what I do, not just on worrying. I'd study for a master's in business part-time, and teach the staff to use the tools. I'd also put some money aside in case the market gets shaken up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe, yes, though ten years is also a long time for things to go wrong somewhere else. I'd say it's a good time to prepare and not to get lazy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though I'd probably cope. It's the one where nobody has a plan and a lot of businesses like ours could be in trouble. What would help is quick support for small businesses and their staff, honest information about what's coming, and apprenticeships so young people learn a craft as well as a tool.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think I'm just lucky with a family business. It's true, but it's also a lot of work, and a lot of pressure. I'd like to make the bakery more than a lucky thing, so that it's something I've built.

headlineQuote: I'd like to make the bakery more than a lucky thing, so that it's something I've built.
portrait: Zoe is 23, a **top graduate** in business administration and finance from Stuttgart, living above her family's bakery.
She uses AI tools every day and treats the family **bakery** as her lab and safety net.
Traditional and pro-business, she believes in learning a **craft** before running a firm.
She stays calm in most worlds, and uneasy only when the **2028** deadline leaves no time.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, where nobody has a plan and small businesses like her family's could struggle.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **support for small businesses** and staff, honest information, and apprenticeships that teach a craft.
